meta.disclaimer: Decision-support for trained harm-reduction volunteers. Not medical advice, not a diagnosis tool. When in doubt, hand over to on-site medics or call 112 (EU) / your local emergency number.
sources: Papaseit E, et al. MDMA interactions with pharmaceuticals and drugs of abuse. Expert Opin Drug Metab Toxicol. 2020;16(5):357–369. doi:10.1080/17425255.2020.1749262

Sarparast A, Thomas K, Malcolm B, Stauffer CS. Drug-drug interactions between psychiatric medications and MDMA or psilocybin: a systematic review. Psychopharmacology. 2022;239:1945–1976. doi:10.1007/s00213-022-06083-y

Liechti ME, Baumann C, Gamma A, Vollenweider FX. Acute psychological effects of MDMA are attenuated by the serotonin uptake inhibitor citalopram. Neuropsychopharmacology. 2000;22(5):513–521. doi:10.1016/S0893-133X(99)00148-7
Richards JR, et al. β-Blockers, cocaine, and the unopposed α-stimulation phenomenon. J Cardiovasc Pharmacol Ther. 2017;22(3):239–249. doi:10.1177/1074248416681644

Dose bands: PsychonautWiki (psychonautwiki.org, CC BY-SA) + TripSit factsheets (drugs.json), both retrieved 2026-08-28; cross-checked, conservative value where they disagree; calibrated against clinical doses (MDMA trials, sodium oxybate/Xyrem SmPC, dexamfetamine SmPC, EFSA caffeine opinion 2015, doi:10.2903/j.efsa.2015.4102)
SmPC/SPC texts of listed medications; Erowid interaction summaries (cross-check only)

substances.name: Alcohol
base: Dehydrates and impairs judgement; the most common co-ingestant in every festival incident.

substances.name: Cannabis (THC)
base: Edibles hit late (1–2 h) — redosing is the classic mistake. Panic/greening-out responds to calm, sugar, quiet.

substances.name: MDMA
base: Overheating and hyponatremia are the main killers: cool-down breaks, sip ~500 ml/h of electrolyte drink — do NOT push large volumes of plain water.

substances.name: Amphetamine / Meth
base: Cardiovascular strain, no sleep, no food; psychosis risk rises with sleep deprivation.

substances.name: Cocaine
base: Short action invites redosing; chest pain in a cocaine user is a medical emergency until proven otherwise.

substances.name: Ketamine
base: Falls and airway risk in a k-hole: get them seated/lying somewhere safe, recovery position if unresponsive.

substances.name: LSD
base: Psychological support > medication for a difficult trip: calm sitter, quiet space, grounding.

substances.name: Psilocybin mushrooms
base: As LSD: difficult experiences are managed with calm presence, not drugs.

substances.name: 2C-B / 2C-x
base: Steep, unpredictable dose–response; treat unknown pills/powders as high-potency.

substances.name: GHB / GBL
base: Extremely steep dose curve — 0.5 ml can separate high from coma. Never combined with alcohol. Sudden deep sleep = monitor breathing continuously.

substances.name: Nitrous oxide
base: Main acute risk is falling / brief blackout — do it sitting down.

substances.name: DXM
base: Strongly serotonergic dissociative hiding in cough medicine; interacts badly with most antidepressants.

substances.name: Mephedrone / cathinones
base: Compulsive redosing pattern; strong cardiovascular + serotonergic load.

substances.name: Opioids (non-prescribed)
base: Respiratory depression kills; pinpoint pupils + unresponsive + slow breathing = give naloxone if your team carries it, call emergency services.

substances.name: Benzodiazepines (non-prescribed)
base: Fake pressed bars may contain potent analogues or fentanyl; blackouts and disinhibition.

substances.name: Synthetic cannabinoids
base: Nothing like natural THC in the field: potency swings wildly between batches — seizures, psychosis, heart strain and sudden collapse all happen. Treat any 'weed that behaves strangely' as a possible synthetic.

substances.name: Kratom
base: Stimulant-like at low amounts, opioid-like at higher ones; sedation and nausea are the usual field picture. Regular users can be physically dependent — sudden stopping adds withdrawal to the mix.

substances.name: Caffeine / energy drinks
base: Masks fatigue and adds cardiovascular load on top of stimulants.

meds.name: SSRI antidepressants
meds.ex: sertraline (Zoloft), escitalopram (Lexapro, Cipralex), citalopram, fluoxetine (Prozac), paroxetine

meds.name: ADHD stimulants
meds.ex: methylphenidate (Ritalin, Concerta), lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse, Elvanse), amphetamine salts (Adderall)

meds.name: Benzodiazepines (prescribed)
meds.ex: alprazolam (Xanax), diazepam (Valium), clonazepam (Klonopin, Rivotril), lorazepam (Ativan), bromazepam

meds.name: Tramadol
meds.ex: Ultram, Tramal; combination products with paracetamol

factors.label: Under 18
factors.note: Minors are hit harder by the same amounts, and you carry a duty of care. Involve on-site medics earlier than you would for an adult.

triggers.note: Any substance in a minor: escalate earlier than you would for an adult, keep them with the team, involve medics at the first warning sign.

factors.label: Over ~50
factors.note: Cardiovascular reserve declines with age; undiagnosed heart or blood-pressure conditions are common.

triggers.note: Stimulants at this age carry meaningfully higher cardiac-event risk — take palpitations and chest discomfort seriously immediately.

factors.label: Low body weight (<60 kg)
factors.note: Standard street doses act like high doses. Effects arrive faster and last longer.

triggers.note: Low body weight raises MDMA exposure per dose AND hyponatremia risk from water-drinking — fluid advice matters double.
Depressant doses overshoot easily at low body weight — watch sedation depth.

factors.label: Female
factors.note: Lower average body water: higher exposure per dose for alcohol and MDMA.

triggers.note: MDMA-related hyponatremia occurs disproportionately in women — keep plain-water intake at sips, prefer electrolytes.

factors.label: Pregnant / possibly
factors.note: Every substance on this list carries fetal risk; the priority is the person in front of you.

triggers.note: Pregnancy + any substance: get medics involved early, and tell them about the pregnancy — it changes their treatment choices.

factors.label: Heart condition / hypertension
factors.note: Known cardiac condition or high blood pressure — the main modifier for every stimulant.

triggers.note: Stimulants on a known heart condition: treat chest pain, irregular pulse or breathlessness as an emergency, not a comedown.
Ketamine raises blood pressure and heart rate transiently.

factors.label: Epilepsy / prior seizures
factors.note: Seizure threshold is the axis to watch: sleep loss, stimulants, and missed anticonvulsant doses all lower it.

triggers.note: Stimulants, DXM, alcohol (especially wearing off), synthetic cannabinoids and kratom all make seizures more likely on top of epilepsy.

factors.label: Psychosis history
factors.note: Personal or strong family history of psychosis or bipolar disorder.

triggers.note: Psychedelics, stimulants and high-THC cannabis can trigger or worsen psychotic episodes in vulnerable people; episodes may not settle when the drug wears off.

factors.label: Awake >24 h
factors.note: Sleep deprivation amplifies everything: seizure risk, psychosis risk, emotional instability, misjudged doses.

triggers.note: Stimulants past 24 h awake: paranoia and stimulant psychosis territory; persuading them to rest beats any other intervention.
Exhaustion makes difficult trips much more likely.

factors.label: Not eaten today
factors.note: Empty stomach: faster, harder alcohol absorption and blood-sugar dips that mimic intoxication.

triggers.note: Alcohol on an empty stomach peaks fast — reassess sedation 30–60 min after the last drink; get food in if cooperative.
Stimulants suppress appetite on top of an empty stomach — weakness, shakiness and collapse late in the night are often just glucose.

factors.label: Little fluid today
factors.note: Dehydration worsens overheating, comedowns, and lithium levels (if they take it).

triggers.note: Dehydration + stimulants/alcohol in a hot crowd: start electrolyte sips now, not when symptoms show.

factors.label: Drinking lots of plain water
factors.note: Litres of plain water without electrolytes is a risk in itself with MDMA (hyponatremia).

triggers.note: MDMA + heavy plain-water intake is the classic hyponatremia setup: confusion, headache, vomiting after 'doing everything right'. Switch to electrolytes, cap intake, watch closely.

factors.label: First time with this substance
factors.note: Unknown individual sensitivity: effects, duration and side effects are unpredictable the first time.

triggers.note: First use: advise starting with a fraction of a usual dose, waiting the full onset time before any redose, and staying near the team.

estimates.label: 1 pill (unknown)
estimates.note: EU pills commonly 150–200 mg MDMA, some 300+ — conservative estimate used

mdma.cal: Clinical anchor: MDMA-assisted therapy trials use 80–120 mg once, in screened adults, in a clinic.
mdma.srcNote: PW heavy 150 mg+; TripSit 175 mg+ — conservative shown.
mdma.redose: Redosing multiplies hyperthermia and next-day toll far more than it extends the high; strongly discourage a second full dose.

estimates.label: 1 line speed (unknown purity)
estimates.note: street speed purity varies enormously — often heavily cut

amphetamine.cal: Clinical anchor: prescribed dexamfetamine tops out around 40–60 mg per DAY, divided.
amphetamine.srcNote: PW oral common 10–25 mg; TripSit 20–50 mg — conservative (PW) shown. Meth bands from TripSit.
amphetamine.redose: Each redose extends the sleepless window — psychosis risk climbs with hours awake, not just mg.

estimates.label: 1 line
estimates.note: a typical line is 30–60 mg; purity unknown

cocaine.srcNote: PW heavy 90 mg+; TripSit 150 mg+ — conservative shown.
cocaine.redose: Short action drives redosing every 30–60 min; the cardiovascular load is cumulative even though the high is not.

estimates.label: 1 line
estimates.note: a fat line can be a k-hole dose for a light or naive user

ketamine.cal: Clinical anchor: sub-anesthetic infusions ~0.5 mg/kg; anesthesia starts around 1–2 mg/kg IV.
ketamine.srcNote: PW nasal common 30–75 mg; TripSit 50–125 mg — conservative shown.
ketamine.redose: Tolerance builds within a session; redosing to chase the first effect leads to k-holes and falls.

estimates.label: 1 tab (unknown)
estimates.note: tabs are typically 80–120 µg but range up to 300+; content unknowable without testing

lsd.srcNote: PW heavy 300 µg+; TripSit 250 µg+ — conservative shown.
lsd.redose: Physiologically forgiving, psychologically not — a second tab mid-trip doubles the duration of a possibly difficult experience.

estimates.label: 3.5 g (an eighth)
estimates.note: a strong dose for most people

mushrooms.srcNote: TripSit dried-gram bands; PW psilocybin-mg bands are consistent (~1% psilocybin content). Potency varies several-fold between batches.
mushrooms.redose: Adding more mid-come-up because 'nothing is happening' is the classic route to an overwhelming trip — onset can take a full hour.

2c-x.srcNote: PW and TripSit closely agree for 2C-B. Bands apply to 2C-B ONLY — other 2C-x differ; snorted is much stronger per mg and very painful.
2c-x.redose: Steep dose–response: the step from strong to overwhelming is a few mg.

estimates.label: 1 small cap GBL (~1 ml)
estimates.note: GBL is roughly 2× as potent per volume as GHB and hits faster — confusing the two causes overdoses

ghb.cal: Clinical anchor: sodium oxybate is prescribed at 2.25–4.5 g per single medical dose. PW: risk of death above ~10 g.
ghb.srcNote: PW heavy 4 g+; TripSit heavy 3.5–5 g, dangerous 7 g+ — conservative shown.
ghb.redose: THE redosing killer: second dose before the first peaks (20–40 min) stacks into sudden unconsciousness. Any redose under 2 h is a red flag.

dxm.cal: Clinical anchor: the antitussive ceiling is 120 mg/DAY — every recreational band is far above medical use.
dxm.srcNote: PW absolute bands; TripSit uses mg/kg (common 2.5–7.5 mg/kg) — both shown via the mg/kg readout.
dxm.redose: Long duration — redosing stacks into delirium territory hours later.

mephedrone.redose: Compulsive redosing is the signature of cathinones — totals of 1 g+ per night are common and drive the serotonergic/cardiac harm.

alcohol.helper: Quick count: beer 0.5 l (5%) ≈ 20 g · small beer 0.33 l ≈ 13 g · strong beer 0.5 l (7%) ≈ 28 g · shot 40 ml (40%) ≈ 13 g · wine glass 150 ml (12%) ≈ 14 g. Add them up.
alcohol.cal: Bands are grams of pure ethanol over the evening; the liver clears roughly 10 g per hour, so the same total inside one hour behaves a category higher.
alcohol.srcNote: Converted from TripSit unit bands (1 unit ≈ 10 g ethanol); danger anchor 120 g+ (poisoning watch).
alcohol.redose: Count grams-per-hour, not totals: roughly 10 g clears per hour.

bandDesc.light: light — mildly relaxed, fully functional, conversation normal
bandDesc.common: common — clearly high: giggly or quiet, red eyes, slowed reactions, snacky; fine with company
bandDesc.strong: strong — very high: heavy sedation or anxiety, time distortion, hard to follow conversation; needs a calm space
bandDesc.heavy: heavy — overwhelmed: for non-regular users expect greening out (pale, sweaty, nauseous, panicky, needs to lie down)
bandDesc.danger: extreme edible amount — hours of distress ahead; not lethal, but treat like a psychedelic crisis: calm sitter, quiet space, time

cannabis.helper: Typical contents: joint ≈ 0.25–0.5 g flower ≈ 30–80 mg THC (smoking absorbs only ~a quarter of it) · gummy/edible piece 5–50 mg THC if unlabelled · dabs/concentrates far higher. When smoked, judge by the person's state, not numbers — it self-titrates within minutes.

estimates.label: 1 gummy (unknown)
estimates.note: unlabelled edibles range 5–50+ mg THC per piece

cannabis.cal: Clinical anchor: prescription THC starts at 2.5 mg; 10 mg is a lot for a naive user.
cannabis.srcNote: Edible bands from clinical/regulatory guidance; smoked left qualitative deliberately.
cannabis.redose: Edibles: NO redosing inside 2 hours — delayed onset is how every edible horror story starts.

caffeine.cal: Clinical anchor: EFSA safe single dose ~200 mg, daily ~400 mg.
caffeine.redose: Counts cumulatively across the whole day — ask about total cans, not the last one.

synth-cann.warn: No dose bands can exist here: potency varies enormously between batches and even within one bag — one puff of a strong batch can act like a heavy dose. Ask what it looked like and how much was smoked, but do not trust numbers; judge by the person's state.

kratom.srcNote: PsychonautWiki/TripSit community bands; potency varies several-fold by strain and vendor, extracts are far stronger per gram.
kratom.redose: Stacked doses build opioid-type sedation and nausea over the day; the stimulant feel of the first dose is a poor guide to the fourth.

nitrous.warn: Dose counting adds little here: the acute risks are falls and oxygen deprivation from many balloons in a row without breaks, or bags/masks. Ask about frequency and setting instead of amounts.

opioids-rec.warn: No meaningful dose bands for street opioids: fentanyl and nitazenes make milligram numbers meaningless — a 'usual' amount of a different batch kills. Treat ANY reported amount as potentially heavy; focus on breathing, pupils, responsiveness, and naloxone readiness.

benzos-rec.warn: No meaningful dose bands for street benzos: pressed bars vary from empty to several-times-normal doses, sometimes with fentanyl or potent analogues (bromazolam). Count pills only to gauge intent; judge severity by sedation level, not reported mg.

SS.name: Serotonin syndrome risk
watch: Tremor, muscle twitching or jerking (especially legs)
Confusion; in severe cases rigid muscles and temperature over 39 °C
donot: Do NOT let them take anything else serotonergic — no MDMA redose, no tramadol, no DXM cough medicine, no St John's Wort
Do NOT wrap them in blankets or warm them if hot
Do NOT give their next antidepressant dose 'to balance it out'
care: Cool, quiet space; remove excess clothing
Small sips of water or electrolyte drink
Stay with them — this can escalate over 1–6 hours
SS.call: Muscle rigidity, temperature over 39 °C / hot to touch, confusion or seizure → call emergency services (112) immediately.

CNSDEP.name: CNS / breathing depression risk
watch: Slow, shallow or irregular breathing; snoring or gurgling sounds
donot: Do NOT give any more sedatives — no benzos (Xanax, Valium), no sleep meds (zolpidem), no alcohol, no sedating antihistamines (Benadryl, Phenergan)
Do NOT leave them alone to 'sleep it off'
Do NOT give coffee or stimulants to 'wake them up'
Do NOT induce vomiting
care: Recovery position, keep airway clear
Check breathing every 2–3 minutes — count breaths
Keep trying to rouse them regularly
CNSDEP.call: Breathing under ~10/min, gaps in breathing, blue lips, or can't be woken → call 112 now. If opioids are involved and your team carries naloxone, use it per your protocol.

CARDIO.name: Cardiovascular strain
watch: Very fast (>140 at rest) or irregular pulse
donot: Do NOT allow more stimulants — including energy drinks and coffee
Do NOT give the person's own beta-blocker or any heart medication to 'slow the heart' — that is a medical decision only
Do NOT put them in a cold shower (shock risk) — cool gradually
care: Calm, quiet, cool space; seated position
Slow breathing together (in 4 s, out 6 s) for panic-driven tachycardia
CARDIO.call: Chest pain lasting more than a few minutes, irregular pulse, fainting, or one-sided weakness/face droop → call 112.

HYPERTHERMIA.name: Overheating & fluid balance
watch: Temperature rising, skin hot to touch
No urination for many hours, or drinking litres of plain water
donot: Do NOT push large volumes of plain water — hyponatremia kills MDMA users; ~500 ml/h sipped, ideally with electrolytes
Do NOT let them keep dancing through warning signs
Do NOT use alcohol to cool down or rehydrate
care: Shade / chill-out, cool-down breaks every 30–45 min of dancing
Electrolyte drink in small sips
Cool neck, armpits, groin with damp cloth if overheated
HYPERTHERMIA.call: Temperature over ~39 °C, hot dry skin, confusion, collapse, or headache + vomiting + confusion after drinking lots of water (possible hyponatremia) → 112.

SEIZURE.name: Seizure risk
watch: Complaints of strange aura, déjà vu, metallic taste
donot: Do NOT restrain a seizing person
Do NOT put anything in their mouth
care: Clear hard objects away, cushion the head
Time the seizure
Recovery position once it stops
SEIZURE.call: Any seizure in this context warrants 112; a seizure lasting over 5 minutes or repeating is a critical emergency.

HTN.name: Hypertensive crisis risk
donot: Do NOT give any medication to lower blood pressure yourself
Do NOT allow any further stimulants or tyramine-rich food/drink (aged cheese, tap beer, red wine)
care: Sit them upright, calm environment
Continuous observation
HTN.call: This combination can raise blood pressure to stroke levels — with a severe sudden headache or chest pain, call 112 immediately.

PSYCH.name: Psychological distress
watch: Talk of harming self or others
donot: Do NOT argue with delusions or 'logic them out' of the trip
Do NOT leave them alone
Do NOT allow more psychedelics or stimulants to 'fix' it
care: One calm sitter, quiet dim space
Grounding: name, place, 'this is a substance, it will pass'
Water, blanket, time
PSYCH.call: Danger to self or others, or psychosis not settling as the drug should wear off → medical/psychiatric help.

HYPOGLY.name: Blood sugar risk
watch: Confusion, aggression, slurred speech that looks like drunkenness
donot: Do NOT assume a diabetic who seems drunk is just drunk — check if they can test glucose
Do NOT give insulin
Do NOT force food or drink into an unconscious person
care: If conscious and cooperative: sugary drink or food, then something starchy
Help them test blood sugar if they have a meter
HYPOGLY.call: Unconscious or not improving within 10–15 minutes of sugar → 112.

alcohol|cannabis.note: In excess, this combination can cause nausea. Effects reinforce each other — start lower than usual.

alcohol|mdma.note: The combination of MDMA and alcohol may increase strain on the cardiovascular system and lead to increased alcohol consumption. MDMA may also impair one's ability to recognize their level of drunkenness, leading to increased alcohol consumption and poor decision-making. Alcohol may also increase the risk of dehydration and hyperthermia (increased body temperature) when combined with MDMA.

alcohol|cocaine.note: Cocaine can decrease some of the intoxicating effects of alcohol, causing some people to drink more than they otherwise would, which leads to greater behavioral and physical health risks. There is also some debate about cocaethylene, a metabolite produced when combining alcohol and cocaine, with some researchers positing that it is more cardiotoxic than cocaine on its own. Use moderation when combining these substances.

alcohol|amphetamine.note: Drinking on stimulants is risky because the sedative effects of the alcohol are reduced, and these are what the body uses to gauge drunkenness. This typically leads to excessive drinking with greatly reduced inhibitions, high risk of liver damage and increased dehydration. They will also allow you to drink past a point where you might normally pass out, increasing the risk. If you do decide to do this then you should set a limit of how much you will drink each hour and stick to it, bearing in mind that you will feel the alcohol and the stimulant less. Extended release formulations may severely impede sleep, further worsening the hangover.

alcohol|ketamine.note: Both substances cause ataxia and bring a very high risk of vomiting and unconsciousness. If the user falls unconscious while under the influence there is a severe risk of vomit aspiration if they are not placed in the recovery position.

alcohol|lsd.note: One substance blunts the other; risk of redosing to compensate.

alcohol|mushrooms.note: One substance blunts the other; risk of redosing to compensate.

alcohol|ghb.note: Even in very low doses this combination rapidly leads to memory loss, severe ataxia and unconsciousness. There is a high risk of vomit aspiration while unconscious.

alcohol|nitrous.note: Both substances potentiate the ataxia and sedation caused by the other and can lead to unexpected loss of consciousness at high doses. While unconscious, vomit aspiration is a risk if not placed in the recovery position. Memory blackouts are likely.

alcohol|2c-x.note: One substance blunts the other; risk of redosing to compensate.

alcohol|dxm.note: Both substances potentiate the ataxia and sedation caused by the other and can lead to unexpected loss of consciousness at high doses. Place the affected individual in the recovery position to prevent vomit aspiration from excess. Additionally, CNS depression can lead to difficulty breathing. Avoid on anything higher than 1st plateau.

alcohol|opioids-rec.note: Both substances potentiate the ataxia and sedation caused by the other and can lead to unexpected loss of consciousness at high doses. Place the affected individual in the recovery position to prevent vomit aspiration from excess. Memory blackouts are likely

alcohol|benzos-rec.note: Ethanol ingestion may potentiate the CNS effects of many benzodiazepines. The two substances potentiate each other strongly and unpredictably, very rapidly leading to unconsciousness. While unconscious, vomit aspiration is a risk if not placed in the recovery position. Blacking out and memory loss is almost certain.

cannabis|mdma.note: Large amounts of cannabis may cause strong and somewhat unpredictable experiences in combination with MDMA. Cannabis should be saved for towards the end of the experience if possible. Effects reinforce each other — start lower than usual.

cannabis|cocaine.note: Stimulants increase anxiety levels and the risk of thought loops which can lead to negative experiences

cannabis|amphetamine.note: Stimulants increase anxiety levels and the risk of thought loops which can lead to negative experiences

cannabis|ketamine.note: Effects reinforce each other — start lower than usual.

cannabis|lsd.note: Cannabis has an unexpectedly strong and somewhat unpredictable synergy with psychedelics.

cannabis|mushrooms.note: Cannabis has an unexpectedly strong and somewhat unpredictable synergy with psychedelics.

cannabis|ghb.note: Effects reinforce each other — start lower than usual.

cannabis|nitrous.note: Effects reinforce each other — start lower than usual.

cannabis|2c-x.note: Cannabis has an unexpectedly strong and somewhat unpredictable synergy with psychedelics.

cannabis|dxm.note: Effects reinforce each other — start lower than usual.

cannabis|opioids-rec.note: Effects reinforce each other — start lower than usual.

cannabis|benzos-rec.note: One substance blunts the other; risk of redosing to compensate.

mdma|cocaine.note: Cocaine blocks some of the desirable effects of MDMA while increasing the risk of heart attack.

mdma|amphetamine.note: This combination of stimulants will increase strain on the heart, may cause some physical discomfort, and has the chance to cause cardiovascular issues. The anxiogenic and focusing effects of stimulants can increase the chance of unpleasant thought loops and make the experience more uncomfortable, this combination raises these chances. Amphetamines will increase the neurotoxic effects of MDMA, in addition to causing further concerns of hyperthermia due to the inherent nature of the combination. It will also raise one's body temperature, also likely making the combination more neurotoxic.

mdma|ketamine.note: No unexpected interactions, though likely to increase blood pressure but not an issue with sensible doses. Moving around on high doses of  this combination may be ill advised due to risk of physical injury. Effects reinforce each other — start lower than usual.

mdma|lsd.note: Effects reinforce each other — start lower than usual.

mdma|mushrooms.note: Effects reinforce each other — start lower than usual.

mdma|ghb.note: Large amounts of GHB/GBL may overwhelm the effects of MDMA on the comedown.

mdma|nitrous.note: Effects reinforce each other — start lower than usual.

mdma|2c-x.note: Effects reinforce each other — start lower than usual.

mdma|mephedrone.note: Risk of serotonin syndrome as both drugs raise serotonin levels. Stimulants also increase the neurotoxic effects of MDMA, in addition to concerns of high blood pressure and unnecessary strain on the heart. As well as potentially causing anxiety and greater physical discomfort due to the combination.

mdma|benzos-rec.note: One substance blunts the other; risk of redosing to compensate.

mdma|caffeine.note: Caffeine is not really necessary with MDMA and increases any neurotoxic effects from MDMA

cocaine|amphetamine.note: This combination of stimulants will increase strain on the heart. It is not generally worth it as cocaine has a mild blocking effect on dopamine releasers like amphetamine

cocaine|ketamine.note: No unexpected interactions, though likely to increase blood pressure but not an issue with sensible doses. Moving around on high doses of this combination may be ill advised due to risk of physical injury.

cocaine|lsd.note: Stimulants increase anxiety levels and the risk of thought loops which can lead to negative experiences

cocaine|mushrooms.note: Stimulants increase anxiety levels and the risk of thought loops which can lead to negative experiences

cocaine|ghb.note: Stimulants increase respiration rate allowing for a higher dose of sedatives than normal. If the stimulant wears off first the opiate may overcome the individual and cause respiratory arrest. Likewise the ghb/gbl can wear off and leave a dangerous concentration of cocaine behind

cocaine|nitrous.note: Effects reinforce each other — start lower than usual.

cocaine|2c-x.note: The anxiogenic and focusing effects of stimulants increase the chance of unpleasant thought loops. The combination is generally unnecessary because of the stimulating effects of psychedelics. Combination of the stimulating effects may be uncomfortable.

cocaine|dxm.note: Both substances raise heart rate, in extreme cases, panic attacks caused by these drugs have led to more serious heart issues

cocaine|opioids-rec.note: Stimulants increase respiration rate allowing for a higher dose of opiates than normal. If the stimulant wears off first then the opiate may overcome the individual and cause respiratory arrest.

cocaine|benzos-rec.note: One substance blunts the other; risk of redosing to compensate.

cocaine|caffeine.note: Both stimulants, risk of tachycardia, hypertension, and in extreme cases heart failure.

amphetamine|ketamine.note: No unexpected interactions, though likely to increase blood pressure but not an issue with sensible doses. Moving around on high doses of this combination may be ill advised due to risk of physical injury.

amphetamine|lsd.note: Stimulants increase anxiety levels and the risk of thought loops which can lead to negative experiences

amphetamine|mushrooms.note: Stimulants increase anxiety levels and the risk of thought loops which can lead to negative experiences

amphetamine|2c-x.note: The anxiogenic and focusing effects of stimulants increase the chance of unpleasant thought loops. The combination is generally unnecessary because of the stimulating effects of psychedelics. Combination of the stimulating effects may be uncomfortable.

amphetamine|dxm.note: Both substances raise heart rate, in extreme cases, panic attacks caused by these drugs have led to more serious heart issues.

amphetamine|opioids-rec.note: Stimulants increase respiration rate, which can allow for a higher dose of opiates normal . If the stimulant wears off first then the opiate may overcome the individual and cause respiratory arrest.

amphetamine|benzos-rec.note: Both can dull each other's effects, so if one wears off before the other it's possible to overdose due to the lack of counteraction One substance blunts the other; risk of redosing to compensate.

amphetamine|caffeine.note: This combination of stimulants is not generally necessary and may increase strain on the heart, as well as potentially causing anxiety and greater physical discomfort.

ketamine|nitrous.note: Effects reinforce each other — start lower than usual.

ketamine|2c-x.note: Effects reinforce each other — start lower than usual.

ketamine|dxm.note: Both substances primarily exert their effects through NMDA antagonism. Currently, there is no evidence regarding mechanisms that might reduce these effects. Effects reinforce each other — start lower than usual.

ketamine|benzos-rec.note: Both substances potentiate the ataxia and sedation caused by the other and can lead to unexpected loss of consciousness at high doses. While unconscious, vomit aspiration is a risk if not placed in the recovery position.

lsd|dxm.note: Effects reinforce each other — start lower than usual.

ghb|opioids-rec.note: The two substances potentiate each other strongly and unpredictably, very rapidly leading to unconsciousness. While unconscious, vomit aspiration is a risk if not placed in the recovery position

ghb|mephedrone.note: Both can dull each other's effects, so if one wears off before the other it's possible to overdose due to the lack of counteraction. ghb|benzos-rec.note: The two substances potentiate each other strongly and unpredictably, very rapidly leading to unconsciousness. While unconscious, vomit aspiration is a risk if not placed in the recovery position.

2c-x|benzos-rec.note: One substance blunts the other; risk of redosing to compensate.

2c-x|caffeine.note: High doses of caffeine may cause anxiety which is less manageable when tripping, and since both are stimulating the combination may cause some physical discomfort.

dxm|opioids-rec.note: CNS depression, difficult breathing, heart issues, hepatoxic, just very unsafe combination all around. Additionally if one takes DXM, their tolerance of opiates goes down slightly, thus causing additional synergistic effects.

dxm|mephedrone.note: Risk of serotonin syndrome as both drugs raise serotonin levels. In addition to concerns of high blood pressure and unnecessary strain on the heart. As well as potentially causing anxiety and greater physical discomfort due to the combination.

dxm|benzos-rec.note: Small doses of benzos can end a bad trip, but both substances potentiate the ataxia and sedation caused by the other and this can lead to unexpected loss of consciousness at high doses. While unconscious, vomit aspiration is a risk if not placed in the recovery position.

dxm|caffeine.note: High doses of caffeine can potentially exacerbate anxiety, especially during a dissociative experience, due to its stimulating effects. This combination might also lead to physical discomfort. However, individual responses to caffeine can vary significantly, often influenced by factors like habitual versus occasional usage.

opioids-rec|mephedrone.note: Stimulants increase respiration rate allowing a higher dose of opiates. If the stimulant wears off first then the opiate may overcome the patient and cause respiratory arrest.

opioids-rec|benzos-rec.note: Central nervous system and/or respiratory-depressant effects may be additively or synergistically present. The two substances potentiate each other strongly and unpredictably, very rapidly leading to unconsciousness. While unconscious, vomit aspiration is a risk if not placed in the recovery position Blackouts/memory loss likely

mephedrone|caffeine.note: This combination of stimulants is not generally necessary and may increase strain on the heart, as well as potentially causing anxiety and great physical discomfort. However, individual responses to caffeine can vary significantly, often influenced by factors like habitual versus occasional usage.

benzos-rec|caffeine.note: One substance blunts the other; risk of redosing to compensate.

alcohol|mephedrone.note: Masks drunkenness; dehydration and next-day crash. Alcohol worsens cathinone comedowns.

cannabis|mephedrone.note: THC can amplify stimulant anxiety and racing thoughts.

cocaine|mephedrone.note: Double stimulant load — additive cardiovascular strain and compulsive redosing.

amphetamine|mephedrone.note: Double stimulant load — additive cardiovascular strain, hyperthermia, psychosis risk with sleep loss.

ketamine|mephedrone.note: Stimulant masks ketamine sedation; watch when the stimulant fades.

nitrous|mephedrone.note: Falls and brief blackout on top of stimulant load; sit down.

2c-x|mephedrone.note: Additive stimulant/serotonergic load with an unpredictable psychedelic — cardiovascular and anxiety risk.

mephedrone|benzos-rec.note: Opposing effects mask each other; benzo redosing during comedown risks oversedation once the stimulant clears.

alcohol|synth-cann.note: Heavy sedation, vomiting and collapse — a common bad-outcome pairing in emergency reports.

cannabis|synth-cann.note: Users often don't know their material is synthetic. THC on top tells you nothing about total dose — treat mixed or unknown 'weed' as synthetic.

mdma|synth-cann.note: Stimulant load on top of a convulsant, psychosis-prone cannabinoid.

amphetamine|synth-cann.note: Agitation, heart strain and paranoia all amplified; seizure risk adds up.

cocaine|synth-cann.note: As with other stimulants — cardiovascular and psychosis load amplified.

mephedrone|synth-cann.note: Stimulant + convulsant cannabinoid — agitation and seizure risk.

lsd|synth-cann.note: Two unpredictable psychoactives — difficult trips and psychotic reactions much more likely.

ketamine|synth-cann.note: Sedation and dissociation stack; falls and vomiting.

ghb|synth-cann.note: Sedation stacks unpredictably with a substance that can itself cause collapse.

nitrous|synth-cann.note: Blackout and fall risk on top of an unpredictable substance; sit down.

dxm|synth-cann.note: Dissociation + delirium-prone cannabinoid — confusion and psychological distress likely.

opioids-rec|synth-cann.note: Additive sedation on an unpredictable base.

benzos-rec|synth-cann.note: Benzos are what medics use for synthetic-cannabinoid agitation — but self-dosed on top, watch sedation depth and breathing.

caffeine|synth-cann.note: Extra heart-rate load and jitteriness on a substance already straining the heart.

synth-cann|kratom.note: Unpredictable convulsant + opioid-type sedation — no data, treat as unsafe.

alcohol|kratom.note: A common real-world pairing that ends in heavy sedation and vomiting; opioid-type breathing depression stacks with alcohol.

mdma|kratom.note: Kratom adds mild serotonergic and stimulant load; watch agitation and overheating.

amphetamine|kratom.note: Additive stimulation at low kratom doses; at high doses kratom's sedation is masked until the stimulant fades.

lsd|kratom.note: Little data; kratom's opioid sedation may blunt or muddle the trip.

mushrooms|kratom.note: Little data; additive nausea is the practical issue.

2c-x|kratom.note: Little data — keep doses of both low.

ketamine|kratom.note: Additive sedation and nausea; vomiting while dissociated is an airway risk.

ghb|kratom.note: Opioid-type sedation + GHB is respiratory-depression stacking.

dxm|kratom.note: Serotonergic + opioid overlap on both sides — agitation, sedation and breathing concerns together.

opioids-rec|kratom.note: Kratom is opioid-active — doses stack into respiratory depression.

benzos-rec|kratom.note: Opioid-type sedation + benzos — breathing and airway watch.

default.note: SSRIs are generally not acutely dangerous with most substances, but they blunt serotonergic drugs — the person may redose chasing an effect that won't come.

mdma.note: SSRIs largely block MDMA's effects (redosing spiral is the practical danger) AND raise serotonin-syndrome risk, especially with redosing or high doses. Case reports of severe outcomes exist.
donot: Do NOT let them redose because 'it isn't working' — that is the SSRI blocking it; more MDMA = more toxicity with no high

dxm.note: High risk of serotonin syndrome — DXM is a strong serotonin reuptake inhibitor itself.

mephedrone.note: Strongly serotonergic stimulant on top of an SSRI — serotonin syndrome risk at recreational doses.

lsd.note: Usually just a markedly weakened trip. Do not redose to 'break through'. No major safety signal.

mushrooms.note: Usually a markedly weakened trip. Do not redose to 'break through'.

2c-x.note: Likely blunted; 2C-x series is less predictable than classic psychedelics.

cocaine.note: Mild serotonergic overlap; mainly cocaine undermines the condition the SSRI treats. Watch mood crash after.

amphetamine.note: Generally tolerated acutely; serotonin risk mainly with methamphetamine or high doses.

opioids-rec.note: Fentanyl and some opioids add serotonergic load; case reports of serotonin syndrome.

kratom.note: Kratom has mild serotonergic and opioid activity — case reports of bad reactions with antidepressants exist; watch for agitation and twitching.

synth-cann.note: Unpredictable on its own; no specific interaction known, but mental-state swings hit people on antidepressants harder.

alcohol.note: Additive impairment and judgement effects; hangover + SSRI can worsen mood swings. Not acutely dangerous at moderate intake.

default.note: As SSRIs, plus a noradrenergic component — adds heart-rate/blood-pressure load with stimulants.

mdma.note: Blunted effect (redose temptation) + serotonin syndrome risk + additive blood-pressure/heart-rate load. Venlafaxine is repeatedly implicated in case reports.

cocaine.note: Both push blood pressure and heart rate up at once.

amphetamine.note: Additive cardiovascular strain; monitor pulse and agitation.

lsd.note: Usually blunted trip; no major safety signal.

alcohol.note: Additive impairment; venlafaxine + heavy drinking raises blood-pressure spikes.

default.note: Old-generation antidepressants: cardiotoxic, lower the seizure threshold, strongly sedating/anticholinergic. Treat any combo more seriously than with SSRIs.

mdma.note: Serotonin syndrome plus arrhythmia risk — TCAs destabilise cardiac conduction; MDMA adds a massive extra load on the heart.

amphetamine.note: Arrhythmia and hypertensive risk; TCAs also lower seizure threshold.

cocaine.note: Both destabilise cardiac conduction (sodium-channel effects) — arrhythmia risk well above either alone.

dxm.note: Serotonin-syndrome risk plus stacked confusion/hallucination (delirium) effects.

alcohol.note: Strong additive sedation; TCA + alcohol is significantly more impairing than either alone.

default.note: MAOIs (including moclobemide) are the single most dangerous medication class for recreational combos. When in doubt, treat any combination as unsafe.

mdma.note: One of the most dangerous festival combinations known — MAOI + MDMA has caused fatal serotonin syndrome and hypertensive crises, including with moclobemide. Absolute avoid; if already taken together, treat as a developing emergency even if they feel fine now.

amphetamine.note: Hypertensive crisis — MAOIs multiply amphetamine's noradrenaline release.

cocaine.note: Hypertensive crisis risk; poorly explored, treat as dangerous.

mephedrone.note: Serotonergic stimulant + MAOI — both serotonin syndrome and hypertensive crisis in play.

alcohol.note: Tyramine in tap beer and red wine can trigger hypertensive reactions with irreversible MAOIs; moclobemide is more forgiving but caution stands.

opioids-rec.note: Certain opioids (pethidine, fentanyl, tramadol-like) have caused severe reactions with MAOIs.

lsd.note: MAOIs may blunt or alter the trip; less dangerous than stimulant combos but unpredictable.

mushrooms.note: MAO inhibition potentiates tryptamines (ayahuasca principle) — trip may be much stronger and longer than expected.

2c-x.note: MAOIs potentiate phenethylamines unpredictably — treat as dangerous.

cannabis.note: Possible potentiation of tachycardia; limited data.

kratom.note: Kratom's monoamine and opioid activity on top of an MAOI is unstudied — treat as unsafe.

synth-cann.note: Unstudied; both unpredictable — treat as unsafe.

caffeine.note: Can add to blood-pressure load; keep intake modest.

default.note: Bupropion lowers the seizure threshold and blocks CYP2D6 (raises blood levels of MDMA, DXM and codeine-type opioids).

amphetamine.note: Stimulant-on-stimulant: cardiovascular load, insomnia, seizure risk.

cocaine.note: Additive stimulant strain and lowered seizure threshold.

mephedrone.note: As with other stimulants — seizure and cardiac risk.

mdma.note: Bupropion raises MDMA blood levels (CYP2D6 block) and adds seizure risk; effects last longer and hit harder than expected.

dxm.note: CYP2D6 block can multiply DXM levels — an 'ordinary' dose can behave like a heavy one.

alcohol.note: Heavy drinking (and especially abrupt withdrawal) plus bupropion raises seizure risk.

default.note: Trazodone and mirtazapine are strongly sedating — the main issue is stacking with other downers.

alcohol.note: Marked additive sedation — a common real-world combo that ends in deep unrousable sleep; airway watch.

ghb.note: Two strong sedatives with steep curves — high risk of unconsciousness and breathing depression.

mdma.note: Trazodone adds some serotonergic load and may blunt MDMA; mirtazapine may blunt it strongly. Low-grade serotonin-syndrome risk, watch for twitching/agitation.

default.note: Lithium has a narrow safety window: festival dehydration, heavy sweating or vomiting RAISES lithium levels. Watch for lithium toxicity (coarse tremor, vomiting, confusion, unsteady gait) in any scenario.
donot: Do NOT let a person on lithium get dehydrated — regular fluids with electrolytes matter more than any single combo rule

lsd.note: Large body of reports of seizures and dangerous trips on lithium + psychedelics — one of the strongest 'do not combine' signals in the psychedelic literature.

mushrooms.note: Same signal as LSD: seizure and psychosis reports.

2c-x.note: Seizure risk as with other psychedelics.

mdma.note: Serotonin-syndrome risk plus MDMA dehydration concentrating lithium — double mechanism.

alcohol.note: Dehydration + vomiting can push lithium toward toxic levels; hydrate with electrolytes.

amphetamine.note: Sweating/dehydration raising lithium levels is the main concern.

cocaine.note: Lithium may blunt cocaine's effects (redose temptation); dehydration concern stands.

synth-cann.note: Convulsant cannabinoid + lithium's own seizure signal with psychoactives — avoid.

default.note: Antipsychotics blunt stimulants and psychedelics (redose temptation), add sedation, and several (quetiapine, olanzapine) prolong QT and drop blood pressure on standing — fainting in heat is common.

alcohol.note: Quetiapine + alcohol is heavily sedating; fainting on standing up in hot crowds.

ghb.note: Strong additive sedation with a steep-curve depressant.

mdma.note: Blunted effect plus QT-prolongation overlap; the practical risk is redosing and arrhythmia in a dehydrated overheated body.

amphetamine.note: Pharmacological tug-of-war: blunted high, redose temptation, arrhythmia overlap with some agents.

cocaine.note: As amphetamine; also lowers seizure threshold with clozapine-type agents.

synth-cann.note: People prescribed antipsychotics are exactly the group synthetic cannabinoids destabilise most — psychosis relapse risk is real; several antipsychotics also lower the seizure threshold.

lsd.note: May blunt or abort the trip (quetiapine is sometimes used that way clinically) — but unsupervised redosing is the risk.

default.note: Generally low acute interaction. The bigger festival risk is MISSED DOSES + sleep deprivation + stimulants lowering the seizure threshold. Carbamazepine speeds up breakdown of many drugs (weaker, shorter effects — redose temptation).
donot: Do NOT let them skip their anticonvulsant doses during the festival

alcohol.note: Heavy drinking and especially next-day withdrawal lower the seizure threshold; valproate adds liver load.

amphetamine.note: Sleep deprivation + stimulants is a classic seizure trigger in people with epilepsy.

mdma.note: Hyponatremia from water-loading is itself a seizure trigger — fluid advice matters double here.

default.note: Prescribed stimulants (methylphenidate, lisdexamfetamine, amphetamine salts) add to any other stimulant's cardiovascular load. Common and mostly uneventful with moderation — but the ceiling is lower for everything stimulating.

mdma.note: Very common combo: additive heart-rate/blood-pressure/temperature load. Lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse/Elvanse) IS amphetamine — effectively double-dosing. Insist on cooling breaks and electrolytes; strongly discourage MDMA redosing.

amphetamine.note: Same class on top of prescribed dose — overdose-range stimulation, insomnia, psychosis risk with sleep loss.

cocaine.note: Additive cardiovascular strain; chest pain must be taken seriously.

caffeine.note: Energy drinks on top of ADHD meds: jitteriness, palpitations, panic. Keep to a minimum.

alcohol.note: Stimulant masks drunkenness — people drink past their limit, then the stimulant wears off first. Watch for sudden collapse late at night.

ketamine.note: Stimulant may mask sedation, inviting ketamine redosing; watch when stimulant fades.

lsd.note: Additive heart-rate load and higher anxiety/thought-loop risk.

synth-cann.note: Stimulant on top of a convulsant, psychosis-prone cannabinoid — agitation, heart strain and paranoia all amplified.

kratom.note: Additive stimulation at low kratom amounts; masking of sedation at high ones.

ghb.note: Stimulant masks GHB sedation — when it wears off, the full depressant load lands at once.

default.note: Non-stimulant but noradrenergic — adds some heart-rate/blood-pressure load; also competes for CYP2D6.

mdma.note: Additive noradrenergic load; possible higher MDMA levels via CYP2D6 competition.

amphetamine.note: Additive cardiovascular load.

default.note: Prescribed benzos behave exactly like street benzos in combos: safe-ish alone, dangerous stacked with other downers.

alcohol.note: The classic blackout combination — strong unpredictable potentiation, rapid unconsciousness, vomit-aspiration risk.

opioids-rec.note: Benzo + opioid is the signature respiratory-depression death combo.

ketamine.note: Additive sedation and ataxia; falls and airway.

benzos-rec.note: Stacking doses of the same class — easy to overshoot into blackout.

amphetamine.note: Opposing effects mask each other; overdose risk when one wears off first.

mdma.note: Benzo blunts the comedown; main issue is sedation once MDMA fades.

synth-cann.note: Benzos are what medics actually use to calm synthetic-cannabinoid agitation — but self-dosed on top, watch sedation depth.

default.note: Zolpidem/zopiclone act on the same receptors as benzos — treat all combos like benzodiazepine combos. Zolpidem alone can cause sleep-walking; with alcohol this gets dangerous.

alcohol.note: Strong potentiation + amnesia/sleep-walking behaviour; vomit-aspiration risk.

kratom.note: Opioid-like sedation stacks with sleep meds.

default.note: Melatonin has no significant dangerous interaction with recreational substances — mild extra drowsiness with depressants at most.

alcohol.note: Mild additive drowsiness; not dangerous.

default.note: Pregabalin/gabapentin potentiate depressants strongly and have their own seizure quirks at high doses.

alcohol.note: Strong, well-documented potentiation — a major factor in pregabalin-related deaths.

opioids-rec.note: Documented multiplier of opioid respiratory depression.

mdma.note: Seizure-risk signal for the combination (TripSit rates it unsafe); stimulant masking of sedation.

amphetamine.note: Seizure-risk signal; stimulant masks sedation, which lands when it wears off.

ketamine.note: Additive dizziness, nausea, loss of consciousness at higher doses.

kratom.note: Gabapentinoids multiply opioid-type breathing depression — kratom counts.

nitrous.note: Additive ataxia/sedation — do it sitting down, watch airway.

default.note: First-generation antihistamines (diphenhydramine, promethazine, doxylamine) are anticholinergic downers: they stack with depressants and add delirium risk at high doses. Promethazine also prolongs QT.

alcohol.note: Strong unpredictable potentiation — rapid unconsciousness.

ketamine.note: Additive sedation, loss of consciousness at high doses.

dxm.note: Serotonin syndrome + delirium + CNS depression — a genuinely bad combination.

mdma.note: Anticholinergics impair sweating — worse heat tolerance while dancing. QT overlap with promethazine.

amphetamine.note: Stimulant masks sedation and delirium warning signs.

cocaine.note: Masking as with amphetamine; respiratory-arrest risk if cocaine wears off first after heavy antihistamine doses.

default.note: Good news: modern allergy meds (cetirizine, loratadine, levocetirizine, desloratadine, fexofenadine) at normal doses have no meaningful dangerous interaction with recreational substances.

alcohol.note: Cetirizine can add mild drowsiness with alcohol; loratadine/fexofenadine barely at all. Not dangerous.

default.note: Tramadol is an opioid AND a serotonin/noradrenaline releaser AND lowers the seizure threshold — it interacts badly with almost everything. Treat any tramadol combo as elevated risk.

alcohol.note: Heavy CNS depression + seizure risk.

mdma.note: Serotonin syndrome + seizures — documented combination.

amphetamine.note: Both lower seizure threshold.

mephedrone.note: Serotonin syndrome and seizure risk at recreational doses.

lsd.note: Tramadol lowers seizure threshold; psychedelics occasionally provoke seizures.

kratom.note: Both lower the seizure threshold, both add serotonergic and opioid load — documented bad combination.

cannabis.note: Mild synergy; not a major safety signal.

default.note: Prescribed opioids (codeine, oxycodone, fentanyl patches) carry the same combo risks as street opioids. Heat can increase fentanyl-patch release.

alcohol.note: Respiratory depression stacking; unexpected loss of consciousness.

ketamine.note: Vomiting + unconsciousness — high aspiration risk outside recovery position.

dxm.note: CNS depression + serotonergic load; DXM also drops opioid tolerance slightly.

cocaine.note: Stimulant masks opioid sedation — respiratory arrest when cocaine wears off first.

amphetamine.note: Masking dynamic as with cocaine.

nitrous.note: Additive sedation; unexpected loss of consciousness at high doses.

kratom.note: Kratom is opioid-active — doses stack with prescribed opioids into deeper sedation and slower breathing.

mdma.note: Masking dynamic; some serotonergic opioids (fentanyl) add serotonin load.

default.note: Key field fact: a person on beta-blockers may NOT show a fast pulse even in serious stimulant toxicity — don't use heart rate alone to judge how bad it is.

cocaine.note: Traditional teaching says beta-blockade + cocaine risks 'unopposed alpha' blood-pressure spikes and coronary spasm; recent reviews dispute how real this is — but chest pain here is an unambiguous 112 call. The masking of tachycardia is the certain problem.
donot: Do NOT give extra doses of their beta-blocker during stimulant use — disputed medicine, strictly a hospital decision

amphetamine.note: Same unopposed-alpha concern and warning-sign masking as cocaine.

mdma.note: Masked tachycardia + reduced exercise tolerance while dancing in heat; fainting risk.

alcohol.note: Both drop blood pressure on standing — fainting in hot crowds; alcohol can hide low-blood-sugar symptoms.

cannabis.note: Both drop blood pressure when standing up — dizziness, falls.

ketamine.note: No major signal at recreational doses.

default.note: Blood-pressure meds + heat + dancing + alcohol = fainting. Diuretics (hydrochlorothiazide, indapamide) also worsen dehydration and electrolyte loss.

mdma.note: Diuretics + MDMA is a genuinely bad pair: dehydration, electrolyte loss and higher hyponatremia risk. Blood-pressure swings both directions.
donot: Do NOT push plain water — electrolyte drinks in sips; this person's sodium balance is already medicated

alcohol.note: Additive hypotension — dizziness, fainting on standing; dehydration.

amphetamine.note: Stimulants push against the medication — blood pressure may spike beyond their controlled baseline.

default.note: The festival pattern — skipped meals, dancing, alcohol — destabilises glucose regardless of the substance. Make sure they eat and can test.

alcohol.note: Alcohol blocks the liver's glucose release: delayed hypoglycemia (often hours later or overnight) that looks exactly like being drunk. On insulin or gliclazide this is the top festival risk for this person.

mdma.note: Appetite suppression + dancing + possible vomiting = glucose chaos; dehydration also matters for metformin.

amphetamine.note: Appetite suppression and missed meals over many hours.

ghb.note: Unconsciousness from GHB vs hypoglycemia can be confused — check glucose if possible, treat breathing first.

default.note: Reliever inhalers interact little — the rule is the opposite: make sure the inhaler is WITH them and reachable.
donot: Do NOT separate the person from their inhaler (lockers, lost bags — check early)

amphetamine.note: Salbutamol + stimulant = additive tachycardia and tremor; still, never withhold the inhaler in an asthma attack.

mdma.note: As amphetamine; dusty dancefloors and smoke are the real triggers.

cocaine.note: Smoked/snorted cocaine irritates airways and can trigger bronchospasm; additive tachycardia with salbutamol.

cannabis.note: Smoking anything can trigger bronchospasm in asthmatics; edibles avoid this.

default.note: No acute dangerous interaction with recreational substances.

alcohol.note: Practical note: vomiting within ~3–4 h of taking the pill can reduce contraceptive protection — worth mentioning if they've been sick.

mdma.note: Same vomiting caveat; no direct interaction.

default.note: Sildenafil/tadalafil drop blood pressure. NEVER combined with poppers/nitrites — that combination causes life-threatening pressure crashes.

cocaine.note: Both strain the heart in opposite blood-pressure directions; combined with cocaine's coronary spasm this raises cardiac-event risk. Chest pain → 112, and tell the crew sildenafil is on board (matters for their treatment).

amphetamine.note: Additive cardiac workload.

mdma.note: Additive cardiac workload; 'sextasy' combo is common — flag the chest-pain rule.

alcohol.note: Additive blood-pressure drop — dizziness, fainting.

default.note: St John's Wort is a real serotonergic drug and enzyme inducer that people forget to mention. Ask about it specifically.

mdma.note: Additive serotonergic load — serotonin-syndrome case reports; also alters MDMA metabolism.
